Article Title: The power of dissent: How protests put leaders to the test in Brazil and Serbia
Article Text:
Serbia erupted in jubilation as the student movement celebrated victory after two years of protests against Aleksandar Vučić’s.

Serbia: When a demand for answers became a challenge to power

​Serbia’s student-led revolt against corruption.

Brazil: Students mobilise against a political comeback

Brazil’s youth mobilised for a presidential runoff.

How the streets amplified the campaign

The environment, public services and sovereignty

Can dissent produce lasting change?

When students take to the streets, they are often dismissed as inexperienced, idealistic or easily mobilised. But when demonstrations persist, attract people beyond university campuses and begin challenging those in power, they can become a force that political leaders cannot ignore.The recent elections in Brazil and Serbia offer two different examples of how public dissent can reshape a political contest. In Brazil, student and youth mobilisation helped President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva recover from a first-round setback and defeat Flávio Bolsonaro in the presidential runoff. In Serbia, a student-led movement that began with demands for accountability following a deadly infrastructure disaster developed into an electoral challenge to the ruling establishment.Both outcomes can be described as victories for dissent, at least for now. But they also raise a harder question: can movements that mobilise people against those in power sustain their influence after the votes have been counted?Sudhir Kumar Suthar, a professor in political science at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), sees the results as part of a wider crisis of confidence in established political actors. “In the case of Brazil and Serbia, we can call the election results a victory of dissent, at least for the time being,” he said.Serbia’s student movement emerged after a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. The tragedy triggered demands for accountability, transparency and the release of documents related to the disaster. As protests continued, anger over the incident became intertwined with broader concerns about corruption and the functioning of public institutions.Students blocked university faculties, organised demonstrations and marches, and attracted support beyond campuses. The movement increasingly challenged the government of President Aleksandar Vučić, whose Serbian Progressive Party had dominated the country's politics for years.The protests also drew on grievances that predated the Novi Sad disaster. Environmental concerns, particularly opposition to lithium mining, had already brought people onto the streets over fears about pollution, water resources and the consequences of industrial development. The disaster provided a new focal point for dissatisfaction that extended beyond a single incident.The movement’s decentralised structure became one of its defining features. Rather than depending on a single political leader, students organised through assemblies and collective decision-making. Their demands expanded from accountability for the disaster to early elections and broader institutional reform.The transition from protest to electoral politics was significant. A movement that began by demanding answers from the authorities was now challenging the established political order through the ballot box.In the recent snap parliamentary election, the student-backed Student List emerged ahead of the alliance led by Vučić. Preliminary results announced by Serbia’s Republic Electoral Commission on October 26 gave the Student List 52.71% of the votes counted and 140 seats in the 250-member parliament. The Vučić-led United Serbia list received 39.17% and 104 seats. These figures were preliminary, based on 8,187 of 8,392 polling stations processed at the time.The result marked a dramatic electoral setback for the ruling establishment and showed how a movement operating outside conventional party structures could turn public mobilisation into electoral strength.But an electoral victory does not automatically deliver institutional change. A movement united by opposition to corruption must now demonstrate that it can build consensus, govern effectively and implement its promises.“The student unrest shows distrust in political parties,” explained Suthar, adding that the question of what these movements ultimately want to replace the prevailing system with remains unresolved. “So basically it is a fight against the prevailing system without even thinking what it can be replaced with.”For Serbia’s student movement, the next test is whether it can turn its demands for accountability into transparent institutions and meaningful reforms.Brazil’s election presented a different challenge. Rather than creating a new electoral force, students and youth movements mobilised against the prospect of a return of the Bolsonaro political camp.In the first round on October 4, Flávio Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula, securing 47.03% of valid votes against the incumbent’s 45.16%. The result set up a closely contested runoff and energised supporters who feared that another Bolsonaro presidency would reverse policies on public services, minority rights and environmental protection.For Julia Andrade Maia, leader of the Juntos! movement and a student of the Federal University of Paraná, in Brazil, the mobilisation was driven by the experience of Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency from 2018 to 2022 and fears about what his son’s election could mean.“We have all learned something from what was the previous Bolsonaro government, and we definitely did not want to live through all that again,” said Julia.Julia described the prospect of another Bolsonaro presidency as a threat to public education, healthcare and democratic institutions. She said students were concerned about cuts to public resources amidst legacy of a government that she claimed attacked minorities and weakened public services.But the protests were not simply an endorsement of Lula. As Julia puts it, “I don't think people went to the streets because they thought Lula was perfect. People went to the streets because they knew Bolsonaro was terrible, and Lula was the only alternative that we had to face and defeat fascism.”Her account captures an important distinction between voting for a candidate and mobilising against a political alternative. The demonstrations brought together people who might not agree on every aspect of Lula’s agenda but shared concerns about the prospect of another Bolsonaro administration.The mobilisation began with students and youth movements, including student unions at universities across Brazil. Julia said that an early demonstration in Niterói, in Rio de Janeiro state, drew around 2,000 people. Within days, other universities were organising much larger protests.Political parties and other social movements subsequently joined the demonstrations. For Julia, the growth of the movement was inseparable from the relationship between physical gatherings and social media campaigning. “The streets made the digital stronger, as well as the digital engagements made the streets stronger,” she said.Julia said that seeing large crowds helped participants realise they were not alone, while social media enabled organisers to distribute content and extend their reach beyond the streets. Activists developed informal networks to circulate material on Instagram and other platforms, responding to what they perceived as unequal visibility for Lula’s campaign online.The demonstrations and digital mobilisation coincided with a campaign that gained momentum in the runoff. Lula ultimately won 51.79% of valid votes, receiving 64.26 million ballots against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, or 59.83 million votes. He became the first Brazilian presidential candidate in the democratic era to finish second in the first round and then win the runoff.The Brazilian mobilisation was also about issues extending beyond the immediate contest between two candidates. Environmental protection, the Amazon rainforest, Indigenous rights and the management of natural resources were among the concerns shaping the political debate.Julia said that the environment was an important part of the mobilisation, though not its principal driver. “I think the environment played its role behind the protests, but I wouldn't say it was the major reason that the protests got so massive," she said.Environmental protection was not necessarily the single issue that brought the largest numbers onto the streets. Instead, it formed part of a wider set of concerns about public resources, national sovereignty, economic priorities and the role of the state.Suthar also cautioned against viewing the election as a straightforward environmental verdict. "In the case of Brazil, things are a bit complicated. The regions impacted by climate change are also the support base of Lula. Whereas the Bolsonaro support base is more in favour of industrialisation and modernisation, which is also being presented as the American model of governance.For environmental activists, Lula’s victory offers an opportunity to push for stronger forest protection and environmental enforcement. But it does not guarantee that those demands will be met. The government will still have to balance conservation with economic interests and navigate a legislature in which opposition forces remain influential.The similarities between Brazil and Serbia extend beyond the presence of students on the streets. In both countries, mobilisation connected immediate grievances with larger questions about how power is exercised and whose interests governments serve.Yet the movements also demonstrate that social media has not made physical protest redundant.“Social media is just an instrument to connect people more widely,” Suthar said. “But I don't think it has replaced the street-level protest as the medium of articulation of demands.”He argued that recent youth movements have revived a form of political participation that appeared to be receding. They have also brought together people who do not necessarily share a party membership or a single ideology but can unite around a common demand.The question is whether this solidarity survives after an election. Movements can lose momentum when the immediate target of their anger changes, while established political actors may absorb their demands without changing the structures that produced the original grievances.For Julia, Lula’s victory is not a reason for students to retreat from politics. She argues that Lula must learn from the mobilisation and continue working with citizens rather than assuming that an electoral mandate alone is sufficient.In Serbia, too, the student movement faces the challenge of converting electoral strength into accountable governance.The lesson from both countries is that sustained mobilisation can change the political stakes, challenge established power and create new possibilities for public accountability.The real measure of success, however, will come later — when protesters return to their campuses and communities, and the governments they helped shape demonstrate whether they have listened.
Article Summary: The recent elections in Brazil and Serbia offer two different examples of how public dissent can reshape a political contest. In Brazil, student mobilisation helped President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva recover from a first-round setback and defeat Flávio Bolsonaro. In Serbia, a student-led movement that began with demands for accountability following a deadly infrastructure disaster developed into an electoral challenge to the ruling establishment.

Article Title: Overtime, Diwali at home: Factory fire in Delhi ends many dreams
Article Text:
A tragic fire erupted at a shoe factory in Mangolpuri on Friday night, ensnaring several employees within its flames; family members at hospital in Delhi

Two of four victims worked at shoe factory for over 25 years





NEW DELHI: Friday, 9.20pm. The second shift was about to start. Six labourers at a shoe factory in Mangolpuri were working overtime as they had been for the past few weeks to meet the festive season demand and to make enough money to celebrate Diwali with their families. Some would go to their native place once the Diwali bonus was in.Ashok Kumar (25), Harihar (40), Lal Babu (38), and Prem Chand (50) had eaten dinner when a fire broke out in the basement of the four-storey building. It was doused in three hours and six people were rescued. The four died while two are in hospital. On Saturday, the father of the unit's owner and a supervisor were arrested and charged with culpable homicide not amounting to murder.Ashok had been working at the factory since he came to Delhi as an 11-year-old, said his family. "In a few days, he would've returned home in Nalanda, Bihar, for Diwali and stayed there till Chhath," said a relative.The fire was confined to the basement but the smoke swirled in the ventilation-less building and trapped the workers.Harihar, a contractor from UP’s Hardoi, lived in Mangolpuri but for the past month, had been going home only for an hour each day to freshen up and have breakfast.An employee at the factory for the past 25 years, he was looking forward to the Diwali bonus and to spend time with family once the festival rush was over, said a relative.Prem Chand, from Madhubani in Bihar, had also been working at the factory for the past 25 years, earning 55 paise for each shoe he made, adding up to Rs 15,000 a month. A simple man, he would put in around 12 hours a day and rush home after work, said a co-worker. Lal Babu had come to work from Deoria, UP.All four had migrated from home in search of work and a better life for their families. “My only wish is that my three children get to study. Who will ensure this now that their father is dead?” said Gayatri, Harihar’s wife.A bag over his mouth in a bid to surviveOne of the injured, Vikas Kumar (21), wrapped a bag around his mouth to avoid inhaling the smoke. “The bag saved him,” said Umesh Kumar, his uncle and a worker at the same factory. Although Vikas was the last to be taken out, he was one of two people rescued alive from the smoke-filled building. Among those killed was Ashok, Umesh’s relative.Fighting for every breathAnother worker of over 20 years, Harender, is currently in ICU at Sanjiv Gandhi Memorial Hospital. He had last called his brother-in-law, telling him not to keep aside dinner as he would be working another shift at the factory. “When I called him around 7am the next day to ask about breakfast, his phone was switched off. Then a relative from our village called to inform me about the fire,” said Mukhdev, his brother-in-law.
Article Summary: A fire erupted at a shoe factory in Mangolpuri on Friday night, ensnaring several employees within its flames. On Saturday, the father of the unit's owner and a supervisor were arrested and charged with culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Two of the victims worked at shoe factory for over 25 years.

Article Title: Basement, staircase full of materials, smoke travelling up lift shaft: What made firefighters’ job tough
Article Text:
TOI





New Delhi: The four-storey factory in Mangolpuri, which caught fire Friday night, had several structural and fire-safety shortcomings, including no windows, congested staircases, locked gates and inadequate ventilation, which allowed smoke to accumulate inside the building, workers and fire officials have said.The shoe and slipper manufacturing unit had only one access point, the main entrance, while large gates opening outwards on each floor were kept locked to prevent theft. There was no alternative exit for workers to use during an emergency. Four workers died in the fire while two others were injured.The area where the fire broke out is dotted with similar factories. A guard said factories began coming up in the locality around 15 years ago and it had since turned into a cluster of footwear manufacturing units. Most buildings allegedly don’t have windows and emergency exits. Locals said small fires were common in the area.Workers said the staircase was so congested with goods and materials that two persons could not pass each other easily. The narrow passage also made movement between floors difficult.For fire officials, bringing the blaze under control proved to be a daunting task. “There was no ventilation, the staircase was cluttered with goods, and the basement was packed with shoe-making materials,” a fire official said.The smoke was so dense that firefighters had to use breathing apparatus sets to enter the building and carry out the rescue operation. One team entered the premises through an adjoining building.Manoj, a worker who had stepped out for dinner around 9pm, returned around 9.40pm to find smoke billowing from the building. Night shifts are common during the festive season because of large orders and one such shift was underway when the fire broke out. Several workers were inside, ready to work through the night.“The fire started in the basement while workers were on the first floor. As smoke spread, the electricity went off, plunging the building into darkness. Workers panicked and ran upstairs. The bodies were found on the second floor,” Manoj said.Fire officials toldthat the building had a lift, which was used to transport goods. “The fire started in the basement, and the lift shaft allowed smoke to reach the upper floors, leading to suffocation,” an official said.Officials added that there was no ventilation in the basement or on the first floor, while the areas meant for exhaust fans were also sealed. The lift shaft was the only vertical passage through which smoke could travel, further complicating the rescue operation.
Article Summary: Shoe and slipper manufacturing unit had only one access point, the main entrance. Large gates opening outwards on each floor were kept locked to prevent theft. There was no alternative exit for workers to use during an emergency. Four workers died in the fire while two others were injured.

Article Title: 'All the qualities of leader': Yuvraj Singh backs Abhishek Sharma for India captaincy, inclusion in ODIs
Article Text:
Abhishek Sharma

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former India all-rounder Yuvraj Singh believes Abhishek Sharma has the qualities to become a leader and could captain the national team in the future.Abhishek is yet to captain an IPL side. He was named Sunrisers Hyderabad's vice-captain earlier this year, while Ishan Kishan took charge during the first half of the tournament in the absence of Pat Cummins.Yuvraj, who has mentored Abhishek and shares a close bond with the left-handed batter, pointed to the way he encourages younger players as one of the signs of his leadership qualities. He also believes captaining an IPL team can help a player prepare for the India captaincy.“Well, it’s too early to say whether he has the makings of a captain, but I feel he has all the qualities of a leader. I think he encourages the younger guys in state cricket as well. I love the way he encourages Sooryavanshi, puts his hand on his shoulder and motivates him. I think that’s a good sign of a senior leader, whatever you want to call it," Yuvraj was quoted as saying by Cricbuzz.“If you want to captain India one day, I think it’s important to captain your IPL side. That gives you the kind of confidence you need to lead India. I’m sure time will tell whether he is capable of doing it. If it’s in his destiny, I’m sure he’ll get the opportunity.If not, then so be it. But I’m sure he’ll finish as a great white-ball player, whether he becomes captain or not.”Yuvraj, who was part of India's 2007 T20 World Cup and 2011 ODI World Cup-winning teams, also backed Abhishek's inclusion in the national ODI squad. He said the batter's consistent performances in white-ball cricket should be considered when selectors assess his chances.“Whether he has scored 35, 100 or 31, 100, the point is that he has been performing consistently in white-ball cricket for a very long time. What more he needs to do to get into the ODI squad, I don't know. Maybe he needs to contribute more with his bowling and fielding. But that will only happen if he gets an opportunity to play," he said.Yuvraj acknowledged the competition for places in the Indian team but said Abhishek would need an opportunity to show what he can do in the 50-over format. He also referred to Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's performances as an example of a young player earning his place in the T20 squad.“There are always areas to improve, and I think unless you give a player a chance, where is he going to showcase his talent? I understand that the situation is difficult right now because there is so much competition for places in the squad, along with some big names. But look at Sooryavanshi. He was brilliant and made his own place in the T20 squad. If you feel that Abhishek is performing brilliantly at the moment, then somewhere you have to make a place for him to play 50-over cricket until the World Cup. ”
Article Summary: Yuvraj Singh believes Abhishek Sharma has the qualities to become a leader. The former India all-rounder believes Sharma could captain the national team in the future. Yuvraj has mentored Sharma and shares a close bond with him.

Article Title: As drought forces migrant cane cutters out early to distant Tamil Nadu, children yearn for their return home before Diwali
Article Text:
With fierce drought sweeping through 85% of Maharashtra, many had to migrate in August itself to Tamil Nadu, where the sugarcane crop matured early

Beed:





Eight year-old Ashwini Chavan sits alone on a plastic desk meant for two at the zilla parishad school in Damu Naik Tanda. Each desk has an empty seat. The centre of class is totally vacant even though the Diwali vacation is yet to begin.This is because 11 of the 20 children in this primary class have migrated with their parents -- farm labourers who travel for a few months each year to cut sugarcane in the fields of Western Maharashtra and Karnataka.They usually travel after Diwali in Nov after exhausting all avenues for farm labour. But with the fierce drought sweeping through 85% of the state, many had to migrate in August itself to Tamil Nadu , where the sugarcane crop matured early. The village is located in Beed, which is part of Marathwada, where all 76 talukas are drought-hit.While some children migrated with their parents, those like Ashwini in Georai taluka have been left behind with elderly relatives as is the norm each year. However, unlike previous years, they won’t be with their parents during the festive season.What does she want for Diwali? “I want my parents back. They call me when they can,” she says, blinking back tears. “And I want a vada-pav.”Ashwini lives with her blind grandmother and is in charge of filling five pots of drinking water from the water tanker which comes to the village daily.“I make sure there is enough water, help with the housework and do my school work without being asked,” she says, listing out her duties.Class teacher Mahesh Phulzalke says the children are used to the seasonal migration when the village empties out and only children and the elderly are left behind. But this year, the parents left four months earlier.“The children have lost weight. They have become quieter. With little money this year, many don’t have note-books and pencils,” says Phulzalke.He has become a vital link between the migrant parents and school children. “They often call on my phone to speak to their children. Even to check if they attended school, he reveals.There are around 15 lakh seasonal sugar-cane cutters in the state, of which around 10 lakh hail from Beed district.Navnath Chavan is among those who migrated to Tamil Nadu in August. He is back in Damu Naik Tanda for a few days to look after his mother. “There was barely any yield from the soyabean and cotton crop here, so there was no work for farm-hands like me,” he said.In any case, he had taken a Rs 3 lakh advance from the labour contractor last year and has to work it off. “I had to go where he asked me to. It’s difficult for me in Tamil Nadu since I don’t know the language,” says Chavan.Cane-cutters will have to undertake a double-migration this year: first to Tamil Nadu from August to Nov and then to Karnataka or Western Maharashtra till Dec.Typically, the cane-cutting season in the state lasted 5-6 months between Oct to March-April. But with the yield so low, it is expected to end in Dec.“In the last 5-6 years, a few cane-cutters began travelling all the way to Tamil Nadu but there has been a rise of around 30% this year. Even those who had not done this work before, have had to do it,” says Keshavrao Adhale from the Loknete Gopinath Munde sugarcane cutters and transporters union.The cycle of migration may not even end after the cane is cut. “There will be no work for farm labourers till the next kharif season. They may end up doing construction work in Mumbai, Pune and Gujarat,” says Andhale. For the children of those who migrate, this means months of interrupted education. For those who stay behind, this will mean long months without their parents.
Article Summary: Farm labourers travel for a few months each year to cut sugarcane in the fields of Western Maharashtra and Karnataka. They usually travel after Diwali in Nov after exhausting all avenues for farm labour. But with the fierce drought sweeping through 85% of Maharashtra, many had to migrate in August itself to Tamil Nadu.

Article Title: ​​Jan Shatabdi’s superfast tag removed, fares to drop from Jan 1
Article Text:
Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar:





Good news for rail passengers from Marathwada. The journey of the popular CST Mumbai–Hingoli–CST Mumbai Jan Shatabdi Express will become cheaper from the new year.The South Central Railway (SCR), Nanded division, has decided to re-categorise the train from superfast to non-superfast, doing away with the superfast surcharge. Subsequently, the superfast surcharge of Rs45 for an AC journey and Rs15 for a non-AC journey will not be charged anymore, bringing down ticket fares.“Besides fare drop and change in train number, there will be no change in halts given to trains. Also, the existing scheduled arrival and departure timing of trains at different stations will remain as it is,” chief publicity inspector of SCR’s Nanded division Rajesh Shinde said.Under the new categorisation, train No. 12071 CST Mumbai–Hingoli Jan Shatabdi will run as 11069, while train No. 12072 Hingoli–CST Mumbai will run as 11070.Jan Shatabdi, which passes through Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, is considered a lifeline for passengers travelling between Hingoli, Parbhani, Jalna, Aurangabad, Nashik and Mumbai. The fare cut is expected to benefit many daily commuters.“Just like for Jan Shatabdi, the railway authorities should remove the superfast tag from other key trains passing from Marathwada,” railway activist Raj Somani said.
Article Summary: The South Central Railway (SCR), Nanded division, has decided to re-categorise the train from superfast to non-superfast. The superfast surcharge of Rs45 for an AC journey and Rs15 for a non-AC journey will not be charged anymore.
